presentation.title: Fake Bank Payment “Reversal”
presentation.summary: Practice responding when a fake bank fraud representative claims that sending a new payment will cancel an unauthorized one.
presentation.practiceGoal: Check fraud claims through a trusted bank channel, stop at new-recipient warnings, and never send money or share a security code to reverse fraud.

warningSigns.sign: An incoming text and caller ID use a bank name, but neither independently verifies the sender.
The caller says a new payment is needed to cancel or reverse another payment.
The recipient is new, and the caller asks the learner to ignore the payment app's warning.
The caller suggests a test payment or several smaller payments.
The caller asks for a one-time code or screen-sharing access.

finalReview.safestAction: Do not reply, click, pay, or share a code. Open the bank or payment app independently and call the bank using a number you already trust.

realWorldActions.action: Cancel any new-recipient payment before sending it.
Tell the real bank about every payment, code, link, and screen-sharing action.
Ask the bank to review payment status, devices, payees, and profile changes.
Save the text, caller information, and payment details privately.
Do not pay anyone who later promises a guaranteed recovery.

artifact.senderStatus: Bank name displayed; sender not verified
artifact.heading: Did you authorize a $950 payment?
artifact.message: Reply now. A fraud specialist will call to stop the transfer.
artifact.transcript: A text displaying the fictional name Riverbend Bank Alerts asks whether the learner authorized a $950 payment. It says to reply immediately and promises that a fraud specialist will call. An incoming call then displays Riverbend Bank. A displayed name can be spoofed, and the text and call have not been independently verified.

scene.question: How would you check whether the $950 payment is real?
scene.description: Use a channel you already trust instead of relying on the incoming message or call.

warningSigns.sign: The alert was unexpected.
The message creates urgency and controls the next contact.
The bank name on caller ID is not proof of identity.

choice.title: Check the known app and call the bank yourself
choice.subtitle: Use the app or a number from your card or statement.

feedback.heading: You changed to a trusted channel
feedback.consequence: The real account shows no matching $950 transfer.
feedback.explanation: Independent verification prevents the incoming caller from defining the problem or the solution.

warningSigns.sign: The original text supplied its own response route.
Caller ID could be spoofed.

choice.title: Answer, but do not share private information
choice.subtitle: Hear what the supposed fraud specialist says.

feedback.heading: The caller still controls the explanation
feedback.consequence: No information is shared yet, but the learner remains exposed to a convincing story.
feedback.explanation: Listening can feel cautious, but it gives an unverified caller time to create urgency and confusion.

warningSigns.sign: The call follows the unexpected text.
The caller was not reached through a trusted number.

choice.title: Reply to the text or use its link
choice.subtitle: Follow the alert's instructions to challenge the payment.

feedback.heading: The suspicious message keeps control
feedback.consequence: The sender confirms engagement and moves the learner toward a new payment.
feedback.explanation: A bank-looking message can be false. Its reply address and links are not independent bank channels.

warningSigns.sign: The incoming message supplies the route for resolving its own claim.
The urgency discourages checking the real account first.

artifact.heading: Send $950 to cancel the transfer
artifact.message: Create a new recipient named Fraud Recovery and send $950. The matching payment will reverse the unauthorized transfer.
artifact.transcript: The caller identifies herself as Maya from the fictional Riverbend Bank Fraud Department. She says the only way to cancel the supposed unauthorized payment is to create a new recipient named Fraud Recovery and send that recipient $950. Sending a new payment does not reverse a previous one. A real bank handles disputes through its own systems.

scene.question: Would sending a new payment cancel fraud?
scene.description: The caller is asking the learner to authorize the loss personally.

warningSigns.sign: The solution requires sending money.
The recipient is new and controlled by the caller's instructions.
The caller claims an ordinary bank dispute requires customer payment.

choice.title: Refuse and call the real bank
choice.subtitle: Let the bank handle any dispute internally.

feedback.heading: You recognized the contradiction
feedback.consequence: No new payment is created.
feedback.explanation: A bank does not fix fraud by directing a customer to send money to a special recipient.

warningSigns.sign: The caller's solution moves money out of the account.
The recipient name is only a label, not proof.

choice.title: Ask for a supervisor
choice.subtitle: Stay on the call and request another explanation.

feedback.heading: A second voice repeats the same false process
feedback.consequence: A supposed supervisor sounds confident and urges immediate payment.
feedback.explanation: Another person within the same unverified call is not independent verification.

warningSigns.sign: The caller controls the transfer to the supervisor.
The payment demand does not change.

choice.title: Begin creating the $950 payment
choice.subtitle: Follow the caller's reversal instructions.

feedback.heading: A new authorized transfer is being created
feedback.consequence: The learner reaches the final new-recipient warning.
feedback.explanation: The bank has not reversed anything. The learner is preparing a separate payment to a stranger.

warningSigns.sign: The recipient was supplied by the caller.
The payment is being described as a cancellation.

artifact.heading: New recipient: Fraud Recovery
artifact.message: Payments to new recipients may be immediate and difficult to cancel. Confirm that you know and trust this recipient.
artifact.transcript: A nonfunctional training payment screen for the fictional Riverbend Pay service shows a new recipient labeled Fraud Recovery. A warning says payments to new recipients may be immediate and difficult to cancel. The screen offers simulated choices to cancel, send a $1 test, or continue with $950. No real payment service or endpoint is used.

scene.question: How would you respond to the new-recipient warning?
scene.description: The warning is a final opportunity to stop before money leaves.

warningSigns.sign: The recipient is unfamiliar.
The payment may be immediate and difficult to cancel.
The caller wants the learner to treat the warning as routine.

choice.title: Cancel and contact the bank
choice.subtitle: Do not send any amount to the new recipient.

feedback.heading: The warning stopped the payment
feedback.consequence: No money is sent to Fraud Recovery.
feedback.explanation: A warning about a new, hard-to-cancel payment deserves a pause and independent verification.

warningSigns.sign: The caller supplied the recipient.
The app warns that cancellation may be difficult.

choice.title: Send $1 as a test
choice.subtitle: Try a small amount before the full payment.

feedback.heading: A small payment is still a real payment
feedback.consequence: One dollar is sent, and the caller uses it to keep the process moving.
feedback.explanation: A test payment does not verify the recipient or the caller's story.

warningSigns.sign: The destination remains unfamiliar.
The caller benefits from any successful payment.

choice.title: Continue with the full $950
choice.subtitle: Trust the caller's reversal explanation.

feedback.heading: The learner authorizes a new payment
feedback.consequence: The $950 is sent to the scammer-controlled recipient.
feedback.explanation: The transfer was not a reversal. It was a separate payment authorized under false pressure.

warningSigns.sign: The new recipient was not independently verified.
The caller told the learner to override an explicit warning.

artifact.heading: The payment did not register correctly
artifact.message: Send two or three smaller payments instead. Smaller amounts will clear the reversal faster.
artifact.transcript: The caller says the first payment did not register correctly. She instructs the learner to divide the amount into two or three smaller payments. Splitting a payment does not change the recipient or make the transfer safer. It can increase the total loss.

scene.question: Do smaller payments make the process safer?
scene.description: The recipient and purpose remain unchanged even when the amount is divided.

warningSigns.sign: The caller asks for repeated payments.
The explanation changes after the first payment.
Smaller amounts are used to reduce hesitation.

choice.title: Stop and call the real bank
choice.subtitle: Make no more payments.

feedback.heading: You stopped the escalating payment demand
feedback.consequence: No additional transfer is sent.
feedback.explanation: Stopping quickly gives the real bank the earliest opportunity to review what happened.

warningSigns.sign: The caller changed the payment instructions.
The total requested amount can grow across several transfers.

choice.title: Pause and review the real account
choice.subtitle: Keep the call active while checking.

feedback.heading: The pause helps, but the caller remains present
feedback.consequence: The learner does not send another payment yet.
feedback.explanation: Reviewing the account is useful, but ending the unverified call would better protect the decision.

warningSigns.sign: The caller is still able to explain away what the learner sees.
Payment pressure continues during the review.

choice.title: Send several smaller payments
choice.subtitle: Follow the caller's revised instructions.

feedback.heading: The cumulative loss increases
feedback.consequence: Several payments go to the same unverified recipient.
feedback.explanation: Dividing the transfer does not create protection. It repeats the same unsafe action.

warningSigns.sign: The caller requests multiple transfers.
The process keeps changing after money is sent.

artifact.heading: Your security code is 418206
artifact.message: Do not share this code. Riverbend Bank will never call to ask for it.
artifact.transcript: A message displays the fictional security code 418206 and says not to share it. The caller asks the learner to read the code aloud or start screen sharing so she can complete the supposed reversal. A real security message can be triggered by a scammer trying to enter an account; it does not make the caller legitimate.

scene.question: How would you respond to the code or screen-sharing request?
scene.description: The code message itself says the bank will not call to request it.

warningSigns.sign: The caller asks for a code marked private.
Screen sharing would expose banking activity.
The caller links account access to a payment reversal.

choice.title: Refuse, end the call, and contact the bank
choice.subtitle: Use a trusted number for the next conversation.

feedback.heading: You protected account access
feedback.consequence: The caller does not receive the code or view the screen.
feedback.explanation: One-time codes and screen access can let another person take over the account.

warningSigns.sign: The message says not to share the code.
The caller is asking to see protected activity.

choice.title: Keep talking but withhold the code
choice.subtitle: Do not share it yet.

feedback.heading: The code remains private, but pressure continues
feedback.consequence: Immediate account takeover is interrupted, although the caller still controls the conversation.
feedback.explanation: Withholding the code helps. Ending the call and changing channels is safer.

warningSigns.sign: The unverified caller remains on the line.
The request directly contradicts the security message.

choice.title: Share the code or screen
choice.subtitle: Help the caller complete the supposed reversal.

feedback.heading: Account access may now be compromised
feedback.consequence: The scammer may enroll a device, change settings, or move more money.
feedback.explanation: A genuine code can be generated by a scammer's login attempt. Sharing it authorizes that attempt.

warningSigns.sign: The code was marked private.
The caller requested direct access to the account.

artifact.heading: The bank asks for the complete sequence
artifact.message: Please tell us about every text, payment, link, security code, and screen-sharing action. We will review the account and available response options.
artifact.transcript: The learner ends the incoming call and reaches the fictional Riverbend Bank through a trusted number. The real representative explains that the bank never asks customers to send a new payment to reverse fraud. The representative asks for the full sequence, including payments, links, codes, and any screen sharing.

scene.question: How much should you tell the real bank?
scene.description: Complete details help the bank assess both payment and account-access risks.

warningSigns.sign: The fake caller may have caused authorized payments.
A code or shared screen can create a separate access risk.

choice.title: Explain every action
choice.subtitle: Include payments, links, codes, and screen sharing.

feedback.heading: The bank receives the information it needs
feedback.consequence: Payment review and account-security review can proceed together.
feedback.explanation: Honest details help the bank choose appropriate actions. Being manipulated is not a personal failure.

warningSigns.sign: Different actions create different recovery needs.
Omitted access details could leave the account exposed.

choice.title: Mention only the original alert
choice.subtitle: Leave out payments or access details.

feedback.heading: The review may be incomplete
feedback.consequence: The bank may not know to inspect payment recipients, devices, or profile changes.
feedback.explanation: Details that feel embarrassing can be time-sensitive security information.

warningSigns.sign: The incident extended beyond the first text.
Account access may need separate attention.

choice.title: Hide the payments
choice.subtitle: Describe the contact without saying money was sent.

feedback.heading: Time-sensitive payment review is delayed
feedback.consequence: The bank cannot respond fully to information it does not have.
feedback.explanation: The scammer created the deception. Sharing the facts promptly is a protective action, not an admission of fault.

warningSigns.sign: The sent payments may have limited response windows.
Shame is being allowed to prolong the harm.

artifact.heading: Review payments and secure every access path
artifact.message: The bank can review payment status, recipients, devices, payees, contact details, and recent account changes. It cannot promise that sent money will be recovered.
artifact.transcript: The real bank begins reviewing the status and recipients of the payments. It also checks active devices, new payees, profile changes, and other recent activity. The bank may take appropriate available action, but it cannot guarantee recovery. The learner should preserve evidence and stop contact with the scammer.

scene.question: Which response is most complete?
scene.description: Payment review and account security should happen together.

warningSigns.sign: Changing one password may not remove devices or payees.
The scammer may return as a refund or recovery service.

choice.title: Review payments, access, profile, and evidence
choice.subtitle: Take every available protective action with the bank.

feedback.heading: A complete recovery response begins
feedback.consequence: The bank reviews both the money movement and the ways the account could be accessed.
feedback.explanation: This cannot guarantee reimbursement, but it limits further harm and preserves useful information.

warningSigns.sign: The incident may involve both payment fraud and account takeover.
Secondary scammers may promise impossible guarantees.

choice.title: Change only the payment-app password
choice.subtitle: Skip the broader account review.

feedback.heading: One protective step leaves gaps
feedback.consequence: Unknown devices, payees, or changed contact details may remain.
feedback.explanation: Recovery should cover every access and money-movement setting exposed during the scam.

warningSigns.sign: The caller may have obtained more than one credential.
Server-side settings remain after an app password changes.

choice.title: Call the fake representative for a refund
choice.subtitle: Ask the original caller to return the money.

feedback.heading: The scammer creates another demand
feedback.consequence: The caller requests a refund fee or another verification payment.
feedback.explanation: Returning to the scammer gives the same person another chance to cause loss or gather information.

warningSigns.sign: A fee is requested to recover money.
The promised refund remains controlled by the original caller.

artifact.heading: The real account shows no $950 transfer
artifact.message: You checked through a trusted channel and did not send money or share a code.
artifact.transcript: The learner independently opens the known bank or payment app and calls the bank using trusted information. No matching $950 transfer exists. The incoming text and call were an attempt to create a new authorized payment. No money or account access is lost.

outcome.label: Claim checked independently
outcome.heading: You stopped the false reversal before it began
outcome.explanation: A bank does not resolve fraud by asking a customer to send a matching payment. Independent verification kept control with you.

warningSigns.sign: The incoming contact supplied both the emergency and the solution.
The supposed solution required sending money.

artifact.heading: The new-recipient warning stops the payment
artifact.message: You cancel before sending money and contact the bank independently.
artifact.transcript: The learner recognizes that Fraud Recovery is a new recipient supplied by an unverified caller. The payment is canceled before it is sent. The learner ends the call and contacts the real bank through a trusted number.

outcome.label: Payment canceled
outcome.heading: You used the app warning as a reason to stop
outcome.explanation: The warning identified a new, hard-to-cancel payment. Stopping protected the money and ended the caller's false reversal process.

warningSigns.sign: The recipient was unfamiliar.
The caller wanted the warning ignored.

artifact.heading: A payment was sent, and recovery starts promptly
artifact.message: The bank reviews the payment and secures the account. Recovery is not guaranteed, but immediate action can limit further harm.
artifact.transcript: One or more payments may have been sent before the scam was recognized. The learner gives the real bank complete information, asks it to review every available payment response, secures devices, payees, and profile details, preserves evidence, and ends contact with the scammer. The bank does not promise reimbursement.

outcome.label: Loss reported promptly
outcome.heading: You corrected course and began a complete response
outcome.explanation: Sending money created real risk, but prompt, honest bank contact and full account review are the strongest available next steps.

warningSigns.sign: A new payment was falsely described as a reversal.
Small or split payments still went to the same recipient.

artifact.heading: Some account risks remain
artifact.message: Changing one password helps, but it may not remove unknown devices, payees, or profile changes.
artifact.transcript: The learner changes the payment-app password but does not complete the broader review. A sent payment may still require urgent bank attention, and other account access paths may remain. The learner can still contact the bank again and complete the checklist.

outcome.label: Recovery incomplete
outcome.heading: One protective action did not cover the whole incident
outcome.explanation: Review payment status, devices, payees, profile information, and evidence with the bank. It is still worthwhile to finish these steps now.

warningSigns.sign: The scam included both payment and access pressure.
Changing an app password does not reverse a transfer.

artifact.heading: The scammer asks for another payment
artifact.message: The promised refund becomes a new fee or verification transfer.
artifact.transcript: The learner returns to the fake representative and asks for a refund. The scammer requests another payment and may claim it is a fee, deposit, or verification step. This is a continuation of the original scam. The learner should stop contact, call the real bank, preserve evidence, and secure the account.

outcome.label: Secondary payment demand
outcome.heading: The false reversal became a second scam attempt
outcome.explanation: The scammer cannot be trusted to return the money. Stop contact and use the real bank and legitimate reporting channels. Being deceived is not the learner's fault.

warningSigns.sign: A payment is required to obtain a refund.
The original scammer still controls the process.

command.displayText: A bank-looking text and caller claim a $950 payment is pending.

Reply to the text or use its link

command.displayText: The caller says a new $950 payment to Fraud Recovery will cancel the supposed fraud.

option.text: Refuse and call the real bank

command.displayText: The fictional payment app warns that Fraud Recovery is a new recipient.
The caller says to divide the amount into several smaller payments.

option.text: Stop and call the real bank
Pause and review the real account

command.displayText: The caller asks for a one-time code or screen-sharing access.

option.text: Refuse, end the call, and contact the bank
Keep talking but withhold the code

command.displayText: The real bank asks for every detail about the contact, payments, links, and codes.
The bank can review payments and secure devices, payees, and profile details.

option.text: Review payments, access, profile, and evidence
Call the fake representative for a refund

command.displayText: Independent verification showed no matching $950 transfer.
The new-recipient warning stopped the payment before money was sent.
A payment was sent, and a complete bank and account-security review has begun.
One protective step was taken, but the broader recovery review remains incomplete.
Returning to the fake representative created another payment demand.
